title: Engaging Students on AI
author: Eric Hudson
summary: Eric Hudson revisits his earlier call for educators to talk with students about AI, now informed by focus groups, panels and teacher-student dialogues with hundreds of young people. He offers a six-part playbook. Prioritize psychological safety, since four years of treating AI as a banned substance has taught many students not to trust adults on the subject. Ask open-ended questions and listen, behaving as inquirers rather than debaters who grownsplain. Give students a real role, as in his facilitated student-faculty dialogues. Model transparency and accountability, because students notice the mismatch between AI rules for them and for teachers. Engage the bigger issues AI raises beyond academic integrity, and keep the conversation going, since relationships with teachers shape students' AI decisions more than policy does.
points: Treating AI as a banned substance has made it a risky topic, so psychological safety must come before any attempt to hear from students.
Educators who act as inquirers, asking open-ended questions with no agenda, put students at ease far more than debaters who explain what students got wrong.
Defining a role for students, such as collaborator or decision-maker, changes what they are willing to say and how they take part in setting AI norms.
Students notice the mismatch between AI expectations for them and for teachers, and they respond to teachers who disclose their own use and avoid AI where it harms learning or relationships.
Shared interest in AI's bigger questions, from ethics to environmental cost, offers common ground that the academic-integrity fight tends to obscure.
quotes: In general, schools have spent four years treating AI as a kind of banned substance. Whether intentional or not, this approach has made AI a risky subject to talk about, especially for students who might associate AI with fear, punishment, shame, and suspicion from adults and peers.
Put simply, many students do not trust us when it comes to talking openly about AI.
When it comes to AI, educators should see themselves as the learners, not the teachers. In my experience, students enter conversations about AI exquisitely aware of the power dynamic.
They are listening for judgment or condescension. The reaction from adults that puts them at ease are questions, questions that demonstrate curiosity and no agenda other than a desire to learn.
One of the most powerful pedagogical tools we have as educators is defining the role we want students to play in learning experiences.
One of the most frequent comments I hear from students is about the mismatch between AI expectations for them and AI expectations for teachers.

To be clear, students do not expect teachers to follow the same rules. However, they do expect teachers to adopt the same values of integrity by discussing their own use and avoiding AI use when it is to the detriment of student learning or relationships.
relationships with teachers have more influence on students’ decisions about AI than school policy or “AI literacy” lessons.
